https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/europe-we.text: Pjotr Sauer Updated Fri, September 4, 2026 at 9:38 AM UTC 0 Freight in front of a Ukrainian Antonov plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport after a drone was spotted nearby.Photograph: NEWS5/AFP/Getty Images Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war. Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe. The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow. That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe. Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home. The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine. But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing. When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024 , it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage. Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path. Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation. Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation. Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other. To counter the shortcoming, several EU states, including the Netherlands, have recently put forward bills that would greatly expand the surveillance powers of the country’s intelligence agencies One area where Europe can point to more tangible action is its growing willingness to detain vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet . On Wednesday, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine’s request. But critics argue that such measures are still not enough to deter Moscow. “Every time we do nothing, we invite Putin to continue,” said one EU lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity. That argument has been made most forcefully by Poland and the Baltic states, which have consistently pushed their western European allies to take a harder line against Moscow. “Hybrid war is not just a nuisance on the internet,” the Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles.” “We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free,” he added. At the same time, Sikorski also appeared to acknowledge, somewhat jokingly, the limits of Europe’s existing toolkit. Recalling Poland’s response to previous suspected Russian operations, he said: “Every time Russia committed arson or tried to blow up a moving train … I closed one Russian consulate, but I ran out of consulates to close.” Jakub Krupa contributed reporting Show comments 0 Advertisement From Our Partners Advertisement Advertisement Mirror UK BBC TV Licence people 'don't realise' £180 refund due – This Morning expert says Mirror UK Barclays and NatWest customers facing immediate extra costs after changes made Express UK Putin's closest ally sends tanks towards NATO's ‘weakest link' as WW3 fears soar Mirror UK Putin humiliated as Russian warplanes burn after Ukraine drones blitz airfield Mirror UK British man dead after car swept away in Spain floods sparking huge rescue effort Mirror UK Benidorm, Magaluf and Ibiza warned of 'significant danger' as severe storms hit Spain Advertisement Contact Feedback Help Cookie Policy EU Digital Services Act Terms and Privacy Policy Your Privacy Choices About Our Ads About Us Sitemap

https://vietnamnews.vn/politics-laws/180.text: Việt Nam, Hungary seek to deepen bilateral ties HÀ NỘI — Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Ngô Lê Văn received Hungarian Ambassador to Việt Nam Baloghdi Tibor in Hà Nội on Thursday, discussing measures to further strengthen and deepen bilateral relations. Văn welcomed the positive developments in the Việt Nam–Hungary Comprehensive Partnership in recent years. He affirmed that amid profound and unpredictable changes in the global situation, Việt Nam has consistently pursued a foreign policy of independence, self-reliance, self-strengthening, diversification and multilateralisation of external relations. Hungary is one of Việt Nam’s leading important partners in Central and Eastern Europe, he said, stressing that Việt Nam attaches importance to and wishes to continuously strengthen multifaceted ties with Hungary. Praising Tibor’s contributions to promoting the Việt Nam–Hungary Comprehensive Partnership, the Deputy FM asked the ambassador and the Hungarian Embassy to continue working closely with the two foreign ministries to urge and support agencies, ministries and sectors of both sides in implementing high-level commitments and agreements. He also called on the ambassador and embassy to give advice on specific orientations and measures to build on the countries’ longstanding traditional friendship, as well as tap new strengths and opportunities for cooperation, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of and deepening bilateral ties across all areas, from politics and diplomacy to economy and trade, investment, science and technology, culture, education and training, healthcare and pharmaceuticals. Tibor thanked the Vietnamese Ministry of Foreign Affairs for its close coordination in recent years. He affirmed that Hungary’s new Government and foreign ministry will continue their policy of attaching importance to and deepening relations with Việt Nam, considering it a priority partner in the region. He agreed that the two sides should continue efforts to promote the Việt Nam-Hungary Comprehensive Partnership and make full use of the coordinating role of the two foreign ministries in the coming period. The two sides agreed to continue close coordination to arrange and promote exchanges and contacts at all levels, particularly the high level, maintain the deputy ministerial-level political consultation mechanism between the two foreign ministries, and effectively leverage the Việt Nam-Hungary Joint Committee on Economic Cooperation. They also agreed to work towards raising bilateral trade to US$2 billion a year, while encouraging businesses of both countries to invest in areas where they have strengths and needs, enabling their economies to complement each other and contributing to greater strategic self-reliance and the long-term, sustainable development interests of both countries. The two sides underscored that education-training is a traditional area of cooperation with considerable potential. More than 3,000 Vietnamese scientists and experts have been trained in Hungary and are now contributing to Việt Nam’s development while serving as a bridge for promoting the countries’ longstanding friendship. They agreed to continue effectively implementing the bilateral agreement on scholarships for Vietnamese students and soon discuss ways to strengthen cooperation in this important field, including the training of officials in law and several other specialised areas. On the occasion, Văn asked Tibor to convey Vietnamese Minister of Foreign Affairs Lê Hoài Trung’s greetings and invitation to visit Việt Nam to Hungarian FM Orban Anita. — VNA/VNS Politics & Law Việt Nam, Laos enhance legal awareness among border village leaders Politics & Law ASEAN Community Vision 2045: From regional commitments to development opportunities for localities Politics & Law PM receives leaders of Lao Front for National Construction, Laos-Việt Nam Friendship Association Politics & Law Vietnamese Prime Minister meets with Lao National Assembly President Politics & Law Việt Nam, Laos seek to deepen strategic cohesion in defence ties Politics & Law Korean Broadcasting System reopens office in Việt Nam Politics & Law Việt Nam ready to work with Canada to build substantive Strategic Partnership: Top leader General Secretary and President Tô Lâm said on its journey to becoming a developed country, Việt Nam hopes to have Canada as a partner, he said, expressing his hope that Canada will see Việt Nam as a natural, close and trusted partner in Southeast Asia.
